title: Completeness, Exponential Families, Ancillarity and Basu
engineName: Estimation and inference — likelihood families, and what makes one rich enough to pin an estimator down
provenance: Review pass, October 2026: 3 per-scene quick checks added on theory, worked and explore scenes from a third-party module review, each read for correctness before import; a further set offered for completion and guided scenes was declined, since those scenes already end with the learner writing an answer. Theory, worked examples and practice authored for this platform against the UGC NET Statistics syllabus. Previous-year questions are stored separately and carry their exam cycle.
objectives: State completeness as a property of a family of distributions, and say why it is not a property of a statistic on its own.
Prove a statistic complete by the standard route: set E[g(T)] = 0, and use uniqueness of a power series, a polynomial or an integral.
Read completeness off the exponential-family form, and recognise a curved family where that argument fails.
Identify an ancillary statistic and apply Basu's theorem to get independence without touching a joint density.
Disprove completeness by constructing a non-trivial unbiased estimator of zero.
Keep sufficient, minimal, complete and ancillary apart — the exam tests the boundaries, not the definitions.

prereq.name: Sufficiency and the factorisation theorem
prereq.why: Completeness is always asked about a sufficient statistic. If finding T is still slow, do the sufficiency topic first.

prereq.name: Expectation of a function of a statistic
prereq.why: Every completeness proof starts by writing E[g(T)] out as a sum or an integral.

prereq.name: Power series and polynomial identities
prereq.why: The proofs all end the same way: a series that vanishes on an interval has every coefficient zero. That step is the whole argument.

refs.title: The Exponential Criterion
refs.why: Puts Bernoulli, Poisson, Normal, Exponential and Geometric into exponential form one at a time. Read it alongside scene 7 if rearranging a density into h(x)c(θ)exp(Σw t) is the step that slows you down.

refs.title: Mathematical Statistics — Exponential Families I and II
refs.why: The natural parameter space and the full-rank condition stated properly. This is the source for the completeness criterion in scene 7, and for why curved families fall outside it.

refs.title: Mathematical Statistics — Unbiased Estimation and Risk Inequalities
refs.why: Where completeness earns its keep: Rao–Blackwell and Lehmann–Scheffé. Reach for it after scene 1, when you want to see the payoff before doing the proofs.

sheet: T is complete if E_θ[g(T)] = 0 for every θ forces g(T) = 0 with probability 1.
Completeness is a property of the FAMILY {f_T(t;θ) : θ ∈ Θ}, never of T by itself.
In words: the only unbiased estimator of zero that is a function of T is zero itself.
That uniqueness is what makes Lehmann–Scheffé give ONE best unbiased estimator.
Proof route: write E[g(T)] = 0, then use uniqueness — power series (Poisson), polynomial (Binomial), differentiate under the integral (Uniform).
Full-rank k-parameter exponential family ⟹ (Σt₁, …, Σt_k) is complete AND minimal sufficient.
Full rank means the natural parameter space contains an open k-dimensional rectangle.
Curved family (dim T > dim θ, e.g. N(θ,θ²)) ⟹ minimal sufficient but NOT complete.
Ancillary: the distribution of A does not depend on θ at all.
Basu: T complete sufficient, A ancillary ⟹ T and A are independent, for every θ.
Complete sufficient ⟹ minimal sufficient (Bahadur). The converse is false.
To DISPROVE completeness, build one non-zero g with E[g(T)] = 0 for all θ — an ancillary function of T minus its mean does it.
cards: If a function of T averages to zero under every θ in the family, that function must be zero.
The family's, not the statistic's. The same T can be complete under one family and not under another.
It makes the unbiased estimator built on T unique, which is what turns Rao–Blackwell into Lehmann–Scheffé.
A power series or polynomial that vanishes on an interval has every coefficient zero.
Full rank — the natural parameter space holds an open k-dimensional rectangle — gives completeness and minimal sufficiency together.
One whose distribution is free of θ. For U(0,θ), X₍₁₎/X₍ₙ₎ is ancillary because θ cancels.
Complete sufficient T is independent of every ancillary A — no joint density needed.
Find a non-trivial g(T) with mean zero for all θ. For U(θ,θ+1), the range minus (n−1)/(n+1) does it.

tricks.hook: Complete = only zero has zero mean
tricks.why: E_θ[g(T)] = 0 for every θ forces g ≡ 0. Nothing non-trivial averages to zero at every θ.
More natural statistics than free parameters → sufficient but NOT complete. N(θ, θ²) is the stock example.
Complete AND sufficient on one side, ancillary on the other. Drop any one and the theorem is gone.
Its distribution does not involve θ, so on its own it says nothing about θ — which frees it to check the model.

shortcuts: Full-rank k-parameter exponential family ⇒ the natural statistic is complete. That is the quickest route there is.
U(θ, θ+1): minimal sufficient (X₍₁₎, X₍ₙ₎), NOT complete — the range is ancillary and spoils it.
Location families: any difference of observations is ancillary. Scale families: any ratio is.
Completeness is a property of the FAMILY, never of one distribution.
remember: Sufficiency reduces the data; completeness makes the reduction unique. They answer different questions.
Check which parameters are actually unknown before quoting Basu — ancillarity is relative to those.

traps: Calling a statistic complete without naming the family it is complete for.
Assuming minimal sufficient implies complete — curved families are the counterexample.
Applying the exponential-family criterion to a family whose support moves with θ.
Forgetting that the natural parameter space must contain an open rectangle, not just two or three points.
Using Basu without checking that T is complete as well as sufficient.
Treating 'ancillary' as 'useless' — an ancillary statistic is exactly what Basu needs, and it can still matter when you condition.
Proving E[g(T)] = 0 for one θ and concluding completeness. It must hold for every θ in Θ.

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four things it will assume
scenes.objective: Check the three pieces of machinery every completeness argument is built from, before the first proof.
body: Completeness is the one idea in this module that looks like pure algebra, and that is exactly what it is: you write E[g(T)] = 0 for every θ and then argue that g must have been zero all along. The argument is short. It is also unforgiving if the algebra underneath is rusty.
Three of these four checks are the algebra. The first is the topic that comes before this one — if it is shaky, finish sufficiency first; this lesson will assume you can produce T without thinking.

items.ask: What does the factorisation theorem say, and why is completeness always asked about a sufficient statistic?
items.recall: If f(x;θ) = g(T(x);θ)h(x) with h free of θ, then T is sufficient. Completeness is a property of the distribution family of T, and it is useful only because of Lehmann–Scheffé — which needs T to be both complete and sufficient.
refresh: Sufficiency says nothing was lost. Completeness says nothing is wasted: the family of distributions of T is rich enough that no non-trivial function of T can average to zero at every θ.

Alone, completeness is a curiosity. Paired with sufficiency it gives uniqueness — one and only one unbiased function of T — and that is what makes an estimator provably best. So every exam question about completeness is really a question about the pair.
If writing down T is still slow, do the sufficiency topic first. Everything here starts after that step.

items.ask: Write E[g(T)] out as an expression, for a discrete T and for a continuous T.
items.recall: Discrete: Σ_t g(t)P(T=t), summed over the support. Continuous: ∫ g(t)f_T(t)dt over the support. Every completeness argument begins by writing one of these and ends by asking what 'this is 0 for all θ' forces on g.
refresh: Expectation of a function of a random variable does not need the distribution of that function. You weight g(t) by the probability of t and add up: that is the law of the unconscious statistician, and it is why no change of variable is needed.
Write the binomial case out in full, because the lesson's first proof is exactly this: E[g(T)] = Σ_(t=0)^n g(t)·C(n,t)p^t(1−p)^(n−t).

And the continuous template, for a one-parameter exponential-family T: E[g(T)] = ∫ g(t)·c(θ)h(t)e^(θt)dt. Setting that to zero for all θ is a statement about a transform of g, which is why these proofs end in a uniqueness argument rather than algebra.

items.ask: A power series Σaₖzᵏ equals zero for every z in an interval. What follows about the coefficients?
items.recall: Every aₖ is zero. A power series that is not identically zero has isolated roots — at most countably many — so it cannot vanish on a whole interval.
refresh: This is the step that finishes almost every completeness proof, so it is worth having a picture of. A nonzero polynomial of degree m has at most m roots; a nonzero power series behaves the same way locally. Vanishing everywhere on an interval is therefore only possible if there was nothing there to begin with.

See it used. For binomial completeness, set E[g(T)] = 0 and divide through by (1−p)ⁿ, which is never zero for p in (0,1). With z = p/(1−p), which sweeps all of (0,∞) as p sweeps (0,1), you are left with Σ_(t=0)^n g(t)C(n,t)zᵗ = 0 for every z > 0.

That is a polynomial in z vanishing on an interval, so every coefficient g(t)C(n,t) is zero, and since C(n,t) > 0, g(t) = 0 for t = 0,…,n. Completeness proved. Notice that the family had to contain enough values of p for z to sweep an interval — the same proof fails if p can only be 1/3 or 1/2.

items.ask: What is the support of a distribution, and why is the conclusion 'g(T) = 0 with probability one' rather than 'g is the zero function'?
items.recall: The support is the set of values T actually takes with positive probability. Completeness forces g to vanish there and says nothing about g anywhere else, so the honest conclusion is P(g(T)=0) = 1 for every θ.
refresh: For a binomial T the support is {0,1,…,n}: the argument pins down n+1 numbers. g(17.5) is simply never consulted, because T never takes that value.

This is not pedantry — it is how a question gets set. 'T is complete, g(T) has expectation zero, therefore g ≡ 0' is a false option; the true one says 'almost surely' or 'with probability one'. Read the options for that phrase.

It also explains why the unbiased function of a complete sufficient statistic is unique only up to sets of probability zero: two estimators that differ nowhere that matters are counted as the same estimator.

scenes.title: A family too rich to hide anything in
scenes.objective: Meet completeness as a statement about a whole family of distributions.
body: Suppose you have a sufficient statistic T, and someone hands you a function g and claims that E[g(T)] = 0. If they mean under one particular θ, that is easy — plenty of non-zero functions average to zero somewhere.
Now make the claim far harder. Insist that E_θ[g(T)] = 0 for EVERY θ in the family. One function, one equation, but the equation has to hold simultaneously across the whole parameter space.

For a rich enough family, that is impossible unless g was zero all along. The distributions of T move around so much as θ varies that no fixed non-zero function can keep averaging to zero against all of them. A family with that property is called complete.

This is why the property belongs to the family and not to T. The same statistic can be complete under one model and fail under another, because what changed was the collection of distributions, not the function of the data.

The payoff is uniqueness. Rao–Blackwell says conditioning an unbiased estimator on a sufficient statistic cannot make it worse. Completeness says there is only one unbiased function of T to land on — so the improvement has a single destination. That is Lehmann–Scheffé, and it is the reason this definition is in the syllabus at all.

aside.h: The phrasing that makes the definition click
aside.body: Read E_θ[g(T)] = 0 ∀θ ⟹ g ≡ 0 as: the only unbiased estimator of zero that depends on the data through T is the trivial one. If a second one existed, you could add it to any unbiased estimator and get a different unbiased estimator — and uniqueness would be gone.

ask.q: Why does 'the only unbiased estimator of zero is zero' force the unbiased estimator built on T to be unique?
ask.nudge: Suppose two different unbiased estimators of θ were both functions of T. What is the expectation of their difference?

scenario.teaser: Why a factory runs two control charts, and why they can be read independently.
scenario.title: The X̄ chart and the R chart, and why Basu lets you trust both
body: A plant machining bearing races measures an internal diameter on five parts every hour. Two charts go up on the wall: an X̄ chart tracking the mean of each sample, and an R chart tracking the range within it. The operator is told to read them separately — a signal on one does not contaminate the other.

That instruction is Basu's theorem wearing overalls. Treat the process as normal with known spread σ while the mean μ drifts. Then X̄ is a complete sufficient statistic for μ. The range R = X₍₅₎ − X₍₁₎ is unchanged if you shift every measurement by a constant, so its distribution does not involve μ at all — R is ancillary.

Complete and sufficient on one side, ancillary on the other: Basu gives independence immediately, with no distribution theory at all. The two charts carry non-overlapping information, which is exactly why a shift in the mean does not inflate the range chart and a widening spread does not drag the mean chart off centre.

The practical payoff is diagnostic. A signal on X̄ alone points at a setting that has moved — tool offset, thermal growth, a changed fixture. A signal on R alone points at variability — a loose spindle, inconsistent material. If the two were dependent you could not read them apart, and every alarm would be ambiguous.
scenario.q: The quality engineer now says σ is also unknown and must be estimated from the same data. Does the independence argument survive?
scenario.answer: The conclusion survives, but this argument does not. With σ unknown, R is no longer ancillary — its distribution depends on σ, which is now a parameter — so Basu cannot be applied in that form. Independence of X̄ and S² for the normal is still true, but it needs the direct distributional proof rather than Basu. This is the trap the exam sets: Basu's hypotheses have to be checked against the parameters actually unknown, not the ones you wish were known.
scenario.link: The same structure underlies residual analysis in regression: residuals are ancillary for the regression coefficients, which is why they are free to be used for checking the model that produced them.

scenes.title: A family of likelihoods that sweeps the whole line
scenes.objective: See the richness that completeness is really asking for.
body: This is the exponential sample again: L(λ) = λⁿ e^(−λΣxᵢ). The data reach it only through n and Σxᵢ, so Σxᵢ is sufficient — that much is the previous topic.

Completeness asks something extra, and it is about the curve rather than the data. Drag λ and notice that the family of densities of T = ΣXᵢ really does move: T is Gamma(n, λ), and as λ runs over all of (0, ∞) the natural parameter −λ sweeps an entire open interval.

That sweep is the condition. A one-parameter exponential family whose natural parameter covers an open interval is full rank, and its sufficient statistic is complete. Nothing non-trivial can average to zero against all of those distributions at once.

Contrast it with a family where λ were allowed only two values. Sufficiency would be unchanged — the likelihood still sees only Σxᵢ — but two equations cannot pin a whole function down, and completeness would fail. Same statistic, different family, different answer.

ask.q: Sufficiency and completeness are both being claimed for Σxᵢ here. Which of the two would survive if λ were restricted to {1, 2}, and which would not?
ask.nudge: Does restricting θ change how the data enter the likelihood? Does it change how many equations E[g(T)] = 0 has to satisfy?

scenes.title: The definition, and the one proof technique
scenes.objective: Hold the definition precisely, and learn the single argument that closes every proof.

blocks.body: A family of distributions {f_T(t; θ) : θ ∈ Θ} is complete if, for every measurable g, E_θ[g(T)] = 0 for all θ ∈ Θ implies P_θ(g(T) = 0) = 1 for all θ ∈ Θ. Loosely, 'T is complete' always means its family is.
The same condition restricted to bounded g. It is weaker, and it is all Basu's theorem actually needs. Exam questions use full completeness; be aware the distinction exists.

1. Write E_θ[g(T)] = 0 explicitly as a sum or integral over t.   2. Strip off every factor that does not involve t.   3. Recognise what is left as a power series, a polynomial, or an integral that must vanish for all θ.   4. Invoke uniqueness: a series vanishing on an interval has all coefficients zero; an integral vanishing for all upper limits has a zero integrand.   5. Conclude g(t) = 0 at every t the statistic can take.

blocks.h: The three endings you will actually use
blocks.body:
Poisson  →  Σ_t a_t λ^t ≡ 0 on an interval ⟹ every a_t = 0
Binomial →  Σ_t a_t r^t ≡ 0 on an interval ⟹ every a_t = 0  (after r = p/(1−p))
Uniform  →  ∫₀^θ g(x)x^(n−1) dx ≡ 0 for all θ ⟹ differentiate in θ ⟹ g ≡ 0

blocks.h: For all θ, not for some θ
blocks.body: The quantifier is the whole content. E[g(T)] = 0 at a single θ says almost nothing. Questions are written so that a candidate who drops the quantifier reaches a confident wrong answer.

blocks.h: Completeness does not follow from sufficiency
blocks.body: Nor from minimal sufficiency. They are separate properties and the exam exploits the gap: a curved exponential family has a minimal sufficient statistic that is not complete. The implication runs the other way — complete and sufficient implies minimal sufficient (Bahadur's theorem) — and the converse is false.

ask.q: In the definition of completeness, why must Eθ[g(T)] = 0 hold for every θ in the parameter space, rather than just one value of θ?
ask.nudge: A single equation may have many non-zero solutions. Completeness requires the zero-expectation condition across the whole family.

scenes.title: Worked in full — Σxᵢ is complete for the Poisson
scenes.objective: See the five steps executed once, with the uniqueness argument spelled out.
scenes.problem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Poisson(λ), λ > 0. Show that T = ΣXᵢ is a complete sufficient statistic for λ.

steps.math: T = ΣXᵢ ~ Poisson(nλ),   P(T = t) = e^(−nλ) (nλ)^t / t!,  t = 0,1,2,…
steps.why: Sums of independent Poissons are Poisson with the parameters added. Completeness is a statement about the family of distributions of T, so you need that family written down before anything else.

steps.say: Write the condition out in full.
steps.math: E_λ[g(T)] = Σ_{t≥0} g(t) · e^(−nλ) (nλ)^t / t! = 0   for every λ > 0
steps.why: Nothing clever — just the definition of expectation for a discrete statistic. The quantifier 'for every λ > 0' is doing all the work and must be carried through.

steps.say: Strip the factor that does not involve t.
steps.math: e^(−nλ) > 0, so divide it out:   Σ_{t≥0} [ g(t) nᵗ / t! ] λ^t = 0   for every λ > 0
steps.why: Dividing by a strictly positive quantity cannot change whether the rest is zero. What remains is a power series in λ with coefficients a_t = g(t)nᵗ/t!.

steps.math: A power series vanishing on an open interval has every coefficient zero:   g(t) nᵗ / t! = 0  for every t
steps.why: This is the step the whole proof exists for. It is only available because the identity holds for a continuum of λ — one value, or even a hundred, would not do it.

steps.math: nᵗ > 0 and t! > 0, so g(t) = 0 for every t = 0,1,2,…   Hence T is complete.
steps.why: g vanishes at every point T can take, which is exactly P(g(T) = 0) = 1. Sufficiency came from factorisation in the previous topic, so T is complete AND sufficient.

scenes.after: Look back at where the family's richness entered: step 4, and nowhere else. Steps 1 to 3 are bookkeeping. If you ever find a proof of completeness that never uses 'for all θ', you have made an error.

ask.q: For a Poisson sample, what is the key step that turns Eλ[g(T)] = 0 for every λ into a statement that each coefficient must be zero?
ask.nudge: Write the expectation as an exponential power series in λ and use uniqueness of its coefficients.

scenes.title: Pause and recall
scenes.objective: Retrieve before reading on — this is where the retention comes from.
scenes.intro: Answer each in your head before revealing. Correcting a wrong retrieval beats re-reading a right answer.

items.a: E_θ[g(T)] = 0 for every θ in Θ implies g(T) = 0 with probability 1.

items.q: Is completeness a property of T, or of something else?
items.a: Of the family of distributions of T. The same statistic can be complete under one family and not under another.

items.q: Which step of a completeness proof actually uses 'for all θ'?
items.a: The uniqueness step — a power series or polynomial vanishing on an interval has every coefficient zero.

items.q: Complete sufficient implies minimal sufficient. Does the converse hold?
items.a: No. A curved exponential family such as N(θ,θ²) has a minimal sufficient statistic that is not complete.

scenes.title: Your turn, with the scaffolding removed — the Bernoulli
scenes.objective: Run the same argument where the ending is a polynomial rather than a power series.
scenes.problem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Bernoulli(p), 0 < p < 1. Show that T = ΣXᵢ is complete.

steps.say: Identify the distribution of T and write the condition.
steps.math: T ~ Binomial(n, p):   E_p[g(T)] = Σ_{t=0}^{n} g(t) C(n,t) p^t (1−p)^(n−t) = 0   for every p ∈ (0,1)
steps.why: A finite sum this time, not an infinite series — which is why the ending will be a polynomial identity rather than a power series one.

steps.say: Divide through by (1−p)^n, which is strictly positive on (0,1).

blank.prompt: Write what the sum becomes. Use r for p/(1−p).
blank.hint: p^t(1−p)^(n−t) ÷ (1−p)^n = p^t(1−p)^(−t) = (p/(1−p))^t. Everything else is unchanged.

steps.why: The substitution turns a two-variable mess into a clean polynomial in a single variable r.

steps.math: As p runs over (0,1), r = p/(1−p) runs over all of (0, ∞)
steps.why: This is the quantifier arriving in its new clothes. The identity now holds on an open interval of r, which is exactly what the uniqueness argument needs.

blank.prompt: What must be true of every coefficient?
blank.hint: A polynomial of degree n that vanishes at infinitely many points is the zero polynomial — so every coefficient vanishes.

steps.why: A non-zero polynomial of degree n has at most n roots. Vanishing on a whole interval leaves only the zero polynomial.

blank.prompt: What does that give for g?
blank.hint: C(n,t) is never zero for t between 0 and n, so the other factor must be.

steps.why: g vanishes at every value T can take, so T is complete. Sufficiency came from factorisation, so T is complete and sufficient — and Lehmann–Scheffé now applies.

scenes.after: Poisson ended in a power series, Bernoulli in a polynomial. Same five steps, different uniqueness theorem at the end. When you meet a new family, the only question is which uniqueness result closes it.

scenes.title: Exponential families, ancillarity, and Basu
scenes.objective: Get completeness without proving it, and get independence without a joint density.

blocks.body: f(x; θ) = h(x) · c(θ) · exp( Σ_{j=1}^{k} w_j(θ) t_j(x) ). The vector (w₁(θ),…,w_k(θ)) is the natural parameter, and the set of values it takes as θ ranges over Θ is the natural parameter space.

blocks.h: The criterion that saves the proof
blocks.body:
If the natural parameter space contains an open k-dimensional rectangle, the family is FULL RANK, and
T = ( Σᵢ t₁(xᵢ), …, Σᵢ t_k(xᵢ) )  is complete AND minimal sufficient.

blocks.h: What full rank is really asking
blocks.body: That the natural parameter genuinely moves in k independent directions. Two isolated values are not an interval; a curve inside a plane is not a rectangle. This is the condition candidates skip, and it is the condition the curved-family questions turn on.

If dim(T) > dim(θ) the natural parameter traces a lower-dimensional curve and the family is not full rank. N(θ, θ²) has T = (ΣXᵢ, ΣXᵢ²) with w₁ = −1/(2θ²), w₂ = 1/θ satisfying w₁ = −w₂²/2 — a curve in the plane, not a rectangle. T stays minimal sufficient and is NOT complete, so Lehmann–Scheffé gives you nothing there.

A statistic A whose distribution does not depend on θ at all. For a location family, the differences Xᵢ − X̄ are ancillary; for a scale family such as U(0,θ), the ratio X₍₁₎/X₍ₙ₎ is ancillary, because θ cancels.
If T is a complete sufficient statistic for θ and A is ancillary, then T and A are independent — for every θ.

It proves independence without anyone computing a joint density. The textbook proof that X̄ and S² are independent for a normal sample is a page of algebra or an orthogonal-transformation argument; Basu does it in three lines. In an exam that is the difference between finishing the question and not.

Sufficient alone will not do, and complete alone will not do. If a question offers a sufficient statistic that is not complete — a curved family, or U(θ,θ+1) — Basu does not apply and any independence you claim is unjustified.

flow.title: Is this statistic complete? And may I use Basu?
flow.alt: Decision chart for completeness and Basu's theorem

nodes.label: You have a sufficient statistic T
Can the density be written in exponential-family form?
Is it FULL RANK: k natural parameters, k free parameters?
Curved family — sufficient but NOT complete
Is the other statistic's distribution free of θ?

flow.note: Full rank is the condition people skip. N(θ, θ²) has a two-dimensional natural statistic for one free parameter — curved, so sufficient but not complete, and Basu does not apply.

scenario.teaser: Why a calibration lab can report a mean and a spread as two unrelated numbers.
scenario.title: Basu's theorem on a calibration certificate
body: A calibration laboratory measures a reference mass ten times and issues a certificate with two numbers: the mean of the readings, and a spread that quantifies the repeatability of the instrument. Everyone treats those two numbers as separate pieces of information — the mean is the measurement, the spread is the uncertainty attached to it.

That separation is a theorem, not a convention. For a normal sample the sample mean is a complete sufficient statistic for μ when σ is known, and the sample variance is ancillary: its distribution does not involve μ at all, since shifting every reading by the same amount leaves the deviations untouched. Basu's theorem then says the two are independent.

Independence is what licenses the practice. It means the spread the lab reports is not quietly contaminated by where the mean happened to land — a high reading does not come packaged with an inflated uncertainty. If the two were dependent, the certificate would have to report a joint statement rather than two numbers, and every downstream calculation that combines uncertainties would need rewriting.

It is also a genuinely normal-distribution fact, not a general one. For an exponential sample the mean and the variance of the sample move together, and no amount of wishing makes them independent. That is why the normality assumption on a calibration certificate is load-bearing rather than decorative.
scenario.close: Ancillary plus complete sufficient gives independence, and independence is what lets two numbers be read separately.

ask.q: What extra property does completeness add to sufficiency, and why does Basu's theorem need both completeness and sufficiency?
ask.nudge: Completeness rules out any non-zero function of the statistic whose expectation is zero for every θ. Basu then pairs a COMPLETE sufficient statistic with an ancillary one; drop completeness and the independence conclusion is not available.

scenes.title: Where completeness is proved by hand, and Basu pays off
scenes.objective: Watch one family give you completeness, ancillarity and independence together.
body: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid U(0, θ). The likelihood is the cliff on screen: θ^(−n) above the sample maximum, zero below. X₍ₙ₎ is sufficient — that was the previous topic — and here it is also complete.

The proof is the third ending from scene 3. X₍ₙ₎ has density n x^(n−1)/θⁿ on (0, θ), so E[g(X₍ₙ₎)] = 0 for all θ becomes ∫₀^θ g(x) x^(n−1) dx = 0 for all θ. Differentiate both sides with respect to θ and you get g(θ)θ^(n−1) = 0 for every θ > 0, so g ≡ 0. The whole argument is one differentiation.

Now look for something ancillary. Take the ratio X₍₁₎/X₍ₙ₎. Scaling every observation by a constant leaves it unchanged, and changing θ is exactly such a scaling — so its distribution cannot involve θ. It is ancillary.
Basu now hands you a fact for free: X₍ₙ₎ and X₍₁₎/X₍ₙ₎ are independent. No joint density, no Jacobian. That is the whole point of the theorem.
Drag the maximum and watch the likelihood move with it while the ratio sits quietly outside the picture, unaffected by θ. Complete sufficient on one side, ancillary on the other, independent by Basu.

ask.q: X₍₁₎ on its own is NOT ancillary for U(0,θ), but X₍₁₎/X₍ₙ₎ is. What does the division actually remove?
ask.nudge: Write X₍₁₎ as θ times a U(0,1) order statistic. Which factor survives the ratio?

scenes.title: Now without the steps — independence in the normal sample
scenes.objective: Choose Basu yourself, and check both of its conditions before you use it.
scenes.problem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid N(μ, σ²) with σ² KNOWN. Prove that X̄ and S² = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²/(n−1) are independent.
hints: Direction — you are being asked for independence, and you have been given a theorem this week that delivers independence. Before reaching for it, write down what it needs: one complete sufficient statistic, and one ancillary statistic. Decide which of X̄ and S² is which.

Method — Basu. X̄ is complete sufficient for μ here, because with σ² known the family is a full-rank one-parameter exponential family. So the work is all on the other side: show that the distribution of S² does not involve μ.
Next step — write Xᵢ − X̄ = (Xᵢ − μ) − (X̄ − μ) and look at what S² becomes. The variables Yᵢ = Xᵢ − μ are N(0, σ²), with no μ in them anywhere.

solution.math: σ² known ⟹ f(x;μ) = h(x)c(μ)exp( (μ/σ²)·Σxᵢ ), a full-rank one-parameter exponential family, so X̄ is complete sufficient for μ.
Xᵢ − X̄ = (Xᵢ − μ) − (X̄ − μ) = Yᵢ − Ȳ,   where Yᵢ = Xᵢ − μ ~ N(0, σ²)
S² = Σ(Yᵢ − Ȳ)²/(n−1), and the distribution of the Yᵢ does not involve μ ⟹ S² is ancillary for μ.
X̄ complete sufficient, S² ancillary ⟹ X̄ ⟂ S², for every μ.

scenes.answer: X̄ is complete sufficient for μ, S² is ancillary for μ, so Basu's theorem gives their independence immediately.
scenes.check: Two conditions were needed and both had to be verified — stating Basu without showing S² is ancillary answers half the question. Note also what the argument assumed: σ² known. The result is true with σ² unknown as well, but Basu alone does not get you there, because then X̄ is no longer sufficient on its own.

scenes.title: Six statements — verdict on each before you look
scenes.objective: Practise the per-statement discipline the real multi-statement items demand.
scenes.intro: Give every statement a true or false verdict first. In the exam these six would be one question scored all or nothing, so a verdict you skipped is a mark you gambled.

items.claim: Completeness is a property of the statistic T alone, independent of the family of distributions.
items.why: False, and the misconception the whole topic rests on. Completeness is a property of the family {f_T(t;θ)}. Restrict Θ enough and the same T stops being complete.

items.claim: If T is complete and sufficient, then T is minimal sufficient.
items.why: True — this is Bahadur's theorem, assuming a minimal sufficient statistic exists. Candidates often believe the converse instead, which is false.

items.claim: Every minimal sufficient statistic is complete.
items.why: False. N(θ, θ²) has minimal sufficient (ΣXᵢ, ΣXᵢ²), which is not complete because the family is curved.

items.claim: The distribution of an ancillary statistic does not depend on θ.
items.why: True — that is the definition. Note it says the distribution, not that the statistic is useless: an ancillary statistic is precisely what Basu's theorem needs.

items.claim: Basu's theorem requires only that T be sufficient and A be ancillary.
items.why: False — T must be COMPLETE and sufficient. Drop completeness and the conclusion fails; U(θ,θ+1) is the standard case where sufficiency holds, completeness does not, and no independence follows.

items.claim: In a full-rank k-parameter exponential family, the natural sufficient statistic is complete.
items.why: True, and it is the shortcut worth memorising: full rank means the natural parameter space contains an open k-dimensional rectangle, and then T is complete and minimal sufficient together.

scenes.title: Transfer — show that a statistic is NOT complete
scenes.objective: Run the argument backwards: construct a counterexample instead of proving a theorem.
scenes.problem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid U(θ, θ+1) with θ ∈ ℝ unknown. The minimal sufficient statistic is T = (X₍₁₎, X₍ₙ₎). Show that T is NOT complete.
hints: Direction — to disprove completeness you do not argue, you exhibit. You need one specific function g, not identically zero, with E_θ[g(T)] = 0 for every θ. Start by asking which functions of T have an expectation that does not move when θ moves.

Method — a function of T whose distribution is free of θ is ancillary, and its mean is therefore some constant c. Subtract the constant and you have your g. So look for an ancillary function of (X₍₁₎, X₍ₙ₎) in this location family.
Next step — the range R = X₍ₙ₎ − X₍₁₎ is unchanged when every observation shifts by the same amount, and changing θ is exactly such a shift. Find E[R], then write down g.

solution.say: Find an ancillary function of T.
solution.math: R = X₍ₙ₎ − X₍₁₎. Shifting all Xᵢ by a constant leaves R unchanged, and the family is a location family, so the distribution of R does not involve θ.
Write Xᵢ = θ + Uᵢ with Uᵢ iid U(0,1). Then R = U₍ₙ₎ − U₍₁₎, and E[U₍ₙ₎] = n/(n+1), E[U₍₁₎] = 1/(n+1), so E[R] = (n−1)/(n+1).
E_θ[g(T)] = E[R] − (n−1)/(n+1) = 0 for EVERY θ, yet g(T) is not identically zero — R is a genuine random variable with positive variance.
A non-zero function of T has mean zero for every θ, so T is not complete. Basu's theorem therefore does not apply to this family.

scenes.answer: g(T) = (X₍ₙ₎ − X₍₁₎) − (n−1)/(n+1) is a non-trivial unbiased estimator of zero, so T = (X₍₁₎, X₍ₙ₎) is not complete.
scenes.check: Two things had to be shown, and a half answer scores nothing: that E[g(T)] = 0 for all θ, AND that g is not identically zero. Candidates routinely produce the function and forget to say why it is non-trivial — which is the half that makes it a counterexample.

scenes.title: What you should now be able to do unaided
scenes.objective: Close the loop before the test.
body: State completeness with its quantifier intact, and say whose property it is.
Prove completeness for a standard family by setting E[g(T)] = 0 and finishing with the right uniqueness result — power series, polynomial, or differentiation under the integral.
Put a density into exponential form, check whether the natural parameter space holds an open rectangle, and take completeness for free when it does.
Spot a curved family by comparing dim(T) with dim(θ), and refuse to claim completeness there.
Identify an ancillary statistic, check both of Basu's conditions, and use it to get independence in three lines.
Disprove completeness by building an ancillary function of T and subtracting its mean.
The mastery test is ten unseen questions across all of this. Hints are off. The pass is 80% overall with 70% floors on the numerical and multi-statement items.

scenes.title: Mastery test
scenes.objective: Demonstrate it independently, on unseen questions.
